title: Small swimmers rotate about their axis, turning a constant swerve into a helical path

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Small swimmers rotate about their axis, turning a constant swerve into a helical path

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Small ciliated and flagellated organisms cannot steer, but by rotating about their long axis while swimming they convert a constant body-fixed swerve into a continually changing direction in space, so they travel along a helix around a nearly straight axis rather than in a circle.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. X: A Parenthetic Note on Geodetics

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: And this axial rotation, just as in the case of a rifle-bullet, causes their natural swerve, which is always in the same direction as regards their own bodies, to be in a continually changing direction as regards space: in short, to make a spiral course around, and more or less approximate to, a straight axial line.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter X, “A Parenthetic Note on Geodetics”; topic “Spiral paths of swimming microorganisms”. Scope: ciliates, flagellates, rotifers, swarm-spores and other small swimming organisms

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch10-06: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.74

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The kinematic mechanism has precise and discriminating predictions, and published open videos cover multiple ciliated and flagellated swimmers. Standard tracking can resolve the core claim, though not every taxon in its broad scope.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Track 3D position and body orientation of swimming microorganisms, estimating axial rotation, body-fixed curvature and helix pitch. The mechanism is supported when observed trajectories follow parameters predicted from rotation and swerve and become circular when rotation approaches zero.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Many videos are two-dimensional.

Phototaxis, boundaries and fluid flow can perturb paths.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.8
operationalizability: 0.9
data existence: 0.7
data adequacy: 0.55
analysis feasibility: 0.8

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Helix versus circle, tied to measured body rotation, is a direct and discriminating test, and some open 3D tracks already exist. They represent a slice of small swimmers rather than the full list of ciliated and flagellated organisms. Reanalysis of those tracks is standard; extending the same test to rotifers and typical ciliates depends on imaging that is only partly archived.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: From 3D tracks, measure body rotation, path curvature and whether the trajectory is a helix about a nearly straight axis rather than a circle. A helix whose turning matches axial rotation supports the swerve-averaging account; circular paths without rotation, or helices produced without body rotation, refute it for that swimmer.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The clearest open 3D tracks are bacteria, whereas the claim centers on ciliates, flagellates, rotifers and swarm-spores.

A helical flagellar beat can draw a helix without a constant body-fixed swerve.
